objective: Connect the Glasgow surname branches into one extended family tree, developing and testing tentative connections from the earliest records first.
common_origin: The owner reports that all men tested share the Glasgow Y-DNA lineage. A shared paternal origin around 1400–1450, possibly earlier, is the working research model; the founder, date and intervening generations remain to be identified.
later_records: Use records after 1850 when they can resolve an earlier identity, migration or branch connection; routine descendant reconstruction is secondary.

metrics.family_heads: Male surname bearers without a father in the selected pedigree and with at least two surname-bearing children; also queue heads with at least two descendants through one child.
metrics.components: Separate paternal components, including isolated surname bearers. Mothers, spouses and marriage connections cannot join surname branches.
metrics.largest_component: Percentage of the selected historical surname cohort in its largest paternal component.
metrics.confidence: Show confidently marked links and the working pedigree separately. Existing tree grades are not a claim that every underlying record has been independently audited.
metrics.baseline: Preserve the initial cohort IDs and input fingerprint. Compare the same surviving baseline people as well as current totals; report additions and missing people separately. Do not improve the score with a virtual founder, invented parent or incompatible alternative fathers.
metrics.target: One connected paternal component and 100% connected pairs in the working pedigree; a complete pedigree can retain one earliest family head. Keep the strongly assessed result separate.

early_connections.title: Glasgow burgess → Stirling John
early_connections.status: Possible identity or earlier family connection
early_connections.basis: The 1447 Glasgow John and the Stirling witness both have burgess descriptions: NRS B66/25/43 groups John Glesgw among burgesses on 8 August 1475. This strengthens the civic comparison. A single career across 1447–1480 is viable; the circa-1450 Stirling birth estimate cannot exclude it. A father–son or other close-family relationship remains an alternative, with no shared holding or kinship clause yet located.
early_connections.next_test: Compare original Glasgow BL68/BL82 with Stirling B66/25/43 and Darow entries for unabridged names, title recitals and endorsements. Distinguish the charter parties’ seals from John’s own identification; no personal seal of Glesgw is established.

early_connections.title: Stirling John → Saltmarket family
early_connections.status: Possible predecessor; degree of relationship open
early_connections.basis: The earlier John is a compatible predecessor to investigate. Estimated profile birth years do not establish identity or a parent–child generation.
early_connections.next_test: Follow title recitals and shared witnesses into the Saltmarket holding; compare the 1506 alias-Smith charter without equating its John to Saltmarket John in advance.

early_connections.title: Place Alan in the earliest family
early_connections.status: Possible close collateral; exact relationship unchosen
early_connections.basis: The existing assessment considers Alan a possible son, brother or nephew of the Stirling John. The proceeding names no relative; choosing one degree would invent precision.
early_connections.next_test: Inspect JC1/1 and the associated remission for Alan's kin or the parties owed satisfaction, then compare those names with the Stirling witnesses.

sources.label: Pitcairn, Criminal Trials I, part I, p. 19

record_references: NRS JC1/1, Jedburgh justice ayre, 26 February 1494/95; year needs manuscript collation

early_connections.title: John → William at Saltmarket
early_connections.status: Leading father hypothesis; already counted as uncertain
early_connections.basis: The same boundaries and four-shilling burden support property succession from John in May 1527 to William by February 1528/29. Father–son succession is the leading family reconstruction; the transfer's kinship clause is missing.
early_connections.next_test: Find the conveyance between 2 May 1527 and 20 February 1528/29; inspect the St Andrew prebend title and NP1/5 or B/10/1/3 margins for heir, son or widow wording.

source_basis: Initial priorities reconcile existing medieval bridge research, the pre-1550 relationship audit and the resolved public catalogue. They are current working comparisons, not newly discovered kinship records.
